cahors: Cahors lies in a meander of the Lot, surrounded by steep, dry limestone hills, 115 km north of Toulouse. It covers 64.72 km2, and its altitude ranges from 105 to 332 metres. It is the historical centre of the Quercy and the main town of the Lot department.

The town's original name was Divona, or Divona Cadurcorum, Divona of the Cadurci. Divona was a fountain, now called the fontaine des Chartreux, worshipped by the Cadurci, a Celtic people of Gaul. They were among the last Celtic tribes to resist the Roman conquest in the 50s BCE. Romanisation was rapid and profound, and Cahors became a large Roman city whose remains include the Arc de Diane, a relic of Roman baths.

In the Middle Ages the town was notorious for financiers known as Cahorsins, Christians who charged interest on loans. The church held that this was the sin of usury, so Cahors became a byword for it, and Dante's Inferno names it alongside Sodom. Pope John XXII, born Jacques Duèze, came from Cahors, the son of a shoemaker. On 7 June 1331 he granted a charter to the University of Cahors, which was annexed to the University of Toulouse in 1751.

The Valentré Bridge, the symbol of the town, was begun in 1308 and finished in 1378. A Devil's Bridge legend is attached to it, and when the bridge was restored in 1879 the architect Paul Gout placed a small sculpture of the devil on one of its towers.

Cahors is the prefecture of the Lot department and the seat of a diocese. Its monuments include the Saint-Étienne cathedral, a national monument, and the Valentré bridge, a World Heritage Site as part of the pilgrimage path to Santiago de Compostela. The wine of the Cahors appellation is a robust, tannic red that must contain at least 70% Malbec.
calabash: The calabash, or bottle gourd (Lagenaria siceraria), is a vine of the family Cucurbitaceae, native to tropical Africa and grown across the tropics. The English word comes from Middle French calebasse and Spanish calabaza, meaning gourd or pumpkin. The gourd was one of the first plants cultivated not mainly for food but for use as containers. Bottle gourds have been recovered from archaeological contexts in China and Japan dating to about 8,000 to 9,000 years ago, while in Africa the earliest record is a gourd reported in 1884 from a 12th Dynasty tomb at Thebes, about 4,000 years old. Genetic and archaeological evidence suggest that it was domesticated independently, first in Asia and over 4,000 years later in Africa.

Calabash fruits take many shapes: huge and round, small and bottle-shaped, or slim and serpentine, and some grow longer than a metre. The fruit can be harvested young and eaten as a vegetable, or left to mature and dried for use as a ladle, bowl, beverage container or musical instrument. The name is also given to the unrelated calabash tree, Crescentia cujete. How the gourd reached the Americas, where it was grown over 8,000 years ago, has long puzzled scholars. A study of 2005 proposed that Paleo-Indians carried it there, but a fuller genetic study of 2014 concluded that American gourds are most closely related to wild African ones and could have drifted across the ocean many times.

Hollowed and dried calabashes are a typical household utensil across West Africa, used to clean rice, carry water and hold food. They are made into instruments such as the Yoruba ṣẹ̀kẹ̀rẹ̀, a rattle similar to a maraca. In many African legends the calabash is a vessel for knowledge and wisdom. Because it is watertight, it was used to ship seeds across the transatlantic slave trade and by enslaved people to carry seeds for planting. In China the hulu is an ancient symbol of health, and in India a dried calabash forms the resonator of the sitar and tanpura.
california: California covers 163,696 square miles and is bordered by Oregon to the north, Nevada to the east, Arizona to the south-east, the Mexican state of Baja California to the south and the Pacific Ocean to the west. In the middle lies the Central Valley, bounded by the Sierra Nevada and the coastal ranges, the state's agricultural heartland. The name most likely comes from the mythical island of California in the 1510 romance The Adventures of Esplandián by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo, whose Queen Calafia ruled a remote land rich in gold and pearls. The name was on a map by 1541. The Spaniards called the peninsula of Baja California Las Californias, and the name spread north to Alta California.

Before European colonisation California was one of the most culturally and linguistically diverse areas of pre-Columbian North America. Historians generally agree that at least 300,000 people lived there, in more than 70 ethnic groups. They managed their environments in complex ways, with forest gardening and controlled burning to prevent destructive wildfires, and political organisation ranged from bands and villages to large chiefdoms on the rich coasts, among them the Chumash, Pomo and Salinan.

European exploration in the 16th and 17th centuries led to colonisation by the Spanish Empire. The area became part of Mexico in 1821. In the Mexican-American War the United States conquered California, and Mexico ceded it in 1848. The gold rush that began that year brought social and demographic changes, among them what has been called the California genocide of the Indigenous peoples. California was admitted as the 31st state in 1850, as a free state, following the Compromise of 1850.

Sacramento is the state capital, and Los Angeles is its most populous city. California is the most populous US state, with over 39 million people. Hollywood has been an important centre of the film industry since the 1920s, and Silicon Valley in the San Francisco Bay Area is a centre of the technology industry.
caliphate: A caliphate is an institution led by a caliph, regarded as a political and religious successor to Muhammad and a leader of the whole Muslim community, the ummah. The word comes from the Arabic khalifah, meaning successor, steward or deputy. Before Islam, Arabian rulers used the title malik, king. After Muhammad's death the Ansar of Medina met in the courtyard of the Banu Sa'ida clan, and at the meeting at Saqifah Abu Bakr was elected the first caliph.

Three major caliphates followed one another in the medieval period: the Rashidun (632 to 661), the Umayyad (661 to 750) and the Abbasid (750 to 1517). After Ali was assassinated by a Kharijite, his son Hasan gave way to Mu'awiyah, who founded the Umayyad dynasty and made the title hereditary. The Umayyad Caliphate took in the Caucasus, Transoxiana, Sindh, the Maghreb and most of the Iberian Peninsula. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads, and their capital Baghdad became a centre of knowledge, culture and trade. The Abbasids lost effective power outside Iraq by about 920, and the Mongols under Hulagu Khan sacked Baghdad in 1258.

The Fatimid Caliphate, from 909 to 1171, was an Isma'ili Shi'i caliphate that began in Tunisia, founded Cairo in 969 and made Egypt its centre. The Ottoman sultans claimed the caliphate from Murad I, and the claim strengthened after Selim I annexed the Mamluk Sultanate of Cairo in 1517 and became defender of Mecca and Medina. The title gained a practical use only in the late 18th century, when it allowed the sultans to answer Russian claims to protect Ottoman Christians. The Ottoman Caliphate was formally abolished in 1924.

Sunni Muslims developed the belief that the caliph is a temporal ruler, elected by the community and bound by Islamic law, and many call the first four caliphs the Rashidun, the rightly guided. Most Shia Muslims hold instead that rulers should be imams chosen by God from the family of the Prophet, descended from Ali. Since the Umayyads every caliphate has been dynastic. Some Sufi orders and the Ahmadiyya movement, which has had caliphs since 1908, use the title for spiritual leaders. Since the 1920s the political caliphate has lain dormant.
cambodia: Cambodia covers about 181,035 km2 and lies entirely within the tropics, with a 443 km coastline along the Gulf of Thailand. Its landscape is a low-lying central plain surrounded by uplands and low mountains, including the Tonle Sap, the Great Lake, and the upper Mekong delta. The Tonle Sap's most distinctive feature is its flooding, from about 2,590 km2 in the dry season to about 24,605 km2 in the rainy season, and the plain around it, devoted to wet rice cultivation, is the heartland of the country.
The highest peak is Phnom Aural, at 1,813 metres. The Khmer name derives from the Sanskrit Kambujadeśa, the land of the sons of Kambu, after a sage from whom the Khmer kings claimed descent.

Cambodia has been inhabited for over 5000 years. The cave of Laang Spean, with radiocarbon dates around 6000 BCE, is considered the most ancient archaeological site in the country, and the first rice farmers came from the north from the third millennium BCE. Iron was worked by about 500 BCE. In the 3rd, 4th and 5th centuries the Indianised kingdoms of Funan and its successor Chenla coalesced in what became Cambodia and southwestern Vietnam, and for more than 2,000 years the region absorbed influences from India and passed them to other Southeast Asian civilisations.

In 802 Jayavarman II declared himself king, uniting the warring Khmer princes of Chenla under the name Kambuja, and the Khmer Empire became the centre of power. Over 600 years it facilitated the spread of first Hinduism and then Buddhism across Southeast Asia. In the 15th century Cambodia declined and lost territory to its neighbours, and during the Post-Angkor period Vietnam and Thailand each attempted to vassalise it. It became a French protectorate in 1863 and secured independence in 1953.

The Khmer Rouge regime carried out the Cambodian genocide from 1975 to 1979 and was deposed by a Vietnamese intervention and occupation, though insurgencies continued until 1999. By 1993 a United Nations peacekeeping mission had restored the monarchy and established a democratic constitution with elections. Cambodia is a constitutional monarchy. About 17 million people live there, 95.8% of them ethnic Khmer.
cambridgeshire: Cambridgeshire is a ceremonial county in the East of England and East Anglia, bordered by Lincolnshire, Norfolk, Suffolk, Essex, Hertfordshire, Northamptonshire and Bedfordshire. The north and east are dominated by the Fens, an extremely flat, drained marsh maintained by drainage ditches and dykes, where Holme Fen is the lowest physical point in the United Kingdom, 2.75 metres below sea level. The south and west are gently undulating. The principal rivers are the Nene, the Great Ouse and its tributary the Cam, which flows through Cambridge.

Must Farm quarry at Whittlesey has been described as Britain's Pompeii for the best-preserved Bronze Age dwellings ever found in the United Kingdom, and many archaeological finds from the Stone Age, the Bronze Age and the Iron Age have come from East Cambridgeshire. Anglo-Saxons settled the area from the fifth century. Genetic testing of seven skeletons from Anglo-Saxon graves at Hinxton and Oakington found that five were migrants or descended from migrants from the continent, one was a native Briton and one had both continental and native ancestry, suggesting intermarriage.

The Domesday Book records the county as Grantbridgeshire, a name related to the river Granta. In 1888 separate county councils were set up for the area around Cambridge and for the liberty of the Isle of Ely. In 1965 these were merged as Cambridgeshire and the Isle of Ely, and under the Local Government Act 1972 this merged with Huntingdon and Peterborough, formed in 1965 from Huntingdonshire and the Soke of Peterborough. The resulting county was called simply Cambridgeshire. Since 1998 Peterborough has been a separate unitary authority.

Because of the flat terrain and the nearness of the continent, many airfields were built in the county in the Second World War for RAF Bomber Command, RAF Fighter Command and the American air forces. The Cambridge American Cemetery and Memorial lies at Madingley.

Peterborough is the largest settlement, and the county also contains the cities of Cambridge and Ely and the towns of Wisbech, Huntingdon and St Neots. Most of it is agricultural. The University of Cambridge, the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world, stands in Cambridge.
camel: The camel is an even-toed ungulate of the genus Camelus, marked by fatty deposits known as humps. Three species survive. The one-humped dromedary makes up 94% of the world's camel population and the two-humped Bactrian camel 6%. The wild Bactrian is a distinct species, not the ancestor of the domestic Bactrian. Camels provide milk, meat, fibre and felt, and are a vital means of transport for passengers and cargo.

The hump is a reservoir of fatty tissue, a reserve of calories and not of water, as is commonly believed. A dromedary can drink as seldom as once every 10 days even in great heat, and can lose up to 30% of its body mass through dehydration.

Camelids originated in North America during the Eocene. Paracamelus, the ancestor of modern camels, crossed the Bering land bridge into Asia during the late Miocene, around 6 million years ago. The camels that stayed in North America were wiped out 10 to 12,000 years ago, when the first indigenous peoples spread there from Asia, although fossils have never been associated with definitive evidence of hunting.

When humans first domesticated camels is disputed. Dromedaries may have been domesticated in Somalia or South Arabia in the 3rd millennium BCE, and the Bactrian in central Asia around 2,500 BCE, as at Shahr-e Sukhteh in Iran. A study of 2016 using mitochondrial DNA suggested that the dromedary was first domesticated in the southeast Arabian Peninsula.

Excavations in the Timna Valley in 2009 to 2013, led by Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef, found what may be the earliest domestic camel bones in Israel or outside the Arabian Peninsula, dating to around 930 BCE. The find drew attention because camels appear in the biblical stories of Abraham, Jacob, Esau and Joseph, and it is taken as strong evidence that those stories were written after that time. The archaeologist William F. Albright had earlier seen the camels of the Bible as an anachronism.

Camels introduced to Australia as transport animals in the 19th and early 20th centuries became a large feral population. The United States Camel Corps experiment of the 19th century also brought camels to the Southwestern United States.
cameroon: Cameroon covers 475,442 square kilometres in Central and West Africa, on the Bight of Bonny, part of the Gulf of Guinea. It is often called Africa in miniature because it has the coast, desert, mountains, rainforest and savanna of the continent. The country divides into five major geographic zones, among them a hot and humid coastal plain and the South Cameroon Plateau, covered by equatorial rainforest.

A chain of mountains, hills and plateaus, the Cameroon range, runs from Mount Cameroon on the coast, the highest point at 4,095 metres, almost to Lake Chad in the north. Volcanism there has created crater lakes. On 21 August 1986 one of them, Lake Nyos, released carbon dioxide and killed between 1,700 and 2,000 people.

Excavations at Shum Laka in the Northwest Region show human occupation dating back 30,000 years. The Baka are counted among the longest continuous inhabitants, and Bantu migrations into eastern, southern and central Africa are believed to have begun from this area about 2,000 years ago. The Sao culture arose around Lake Chad about 500 CE and gave way to Kanem and its successor, the Bornu Empire, while kingdoms, fondoms and chiefdoms arose in the west. Portuguese sailors reached the coast in 1472 and named the Wouri River Rio dos Camarões, the Shrimp River, after the ghost shrimp they found there. In 1896 Sultan Ibrahim Njoya created the Bamum script for the Bamum language.

Germany built a warehouse on the Wouri estuary in 1868, and in 1884 the German Empire claimed the territory as the colony of Kamerun after Gustav Nachtigal made a treaty with a local king. The people resisted in the Bafut Wars and Adamawa Wars. Commercial companies ran local administration and used forced labour on banana, rubber, palm oil and cocoa plantations, a policy criticised by other colonial powers. After World War I the territory was divided between France and the United Kingdom as League of Nations mandates. The French-administered part became independent as the Republic of Cameroun in 1960 under Ahmadou Ahidjo, and the southern part of British Cameroons federated with it in 1961.

Yaoundé is the capital and Douala, the economic capital and main seaport, is among the largest cities. Cameroon is a unitary presidential republic. Its official languages are French and English, and its people speak some 250 native languages. Christianity is the majority religion, with significant minorities practising Islam and traditional faiths. Cameroon is a member of the African Union, the United Nations, the Commonwealth of Nations and the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie.
camille-pissarro: Jacob Abraham Camille Pissarro was born on 10 July 1830 at Charlotte Amalie to Frederick Abraham Gabriel Pissarro, a merchant of Portuguese Jewish descent who held French nationality, and Rachel Manzano-Pomié. His father's marriage to his late uncle's widow caused a stir in the small Jewish community, and the four children were sent to an all-black primary school. In 1855, at 25, Camille moved to Paris and worked as an assistant to the painter Anton Melbye. He found the teaching at the École des Beaux-Arts and the Académie Suisse stifling and asked Corot for instruction instead.

His first painting was accepted by the Paris Salon in 1859. Corot inspired him to paint outdoors, and at the Académie Suisse he met Claude Monet, Armand Guillaumin and Paul Cézanne, who shared his dissatisfaction with the Salon. During the Franco-Prussian War he moved his family to Norwood near London, since he had only Danish nationality. Of the 1,500 paintings he left in France, only 40 remained, since soldiers had used many as floor mats. In 1871 he married Julie Vellay, with whom he had seven children, six of them painters. The family settled at Éragny-sur-Epte in April 1884.

The first Impressionist exhibition, in 1874, shocked critics, who found the subjects vulgar and the brushwork sketchy. Pissarro showed five landscapes, and Émile Zola praised them. In 1885 he met Georges Seurat and Paul Signac and for about three years used their method of small dabs of pure colour, showing such works in 1886 at the eighth exhibition. By the end of the 1880s he found the method too restrictive, but kept a stronger attention to colour. He was also drawn to anarchist circles, and in 1889 made an album of thirty drawings, Turpitudes sociales.

In 1892 Monet helped Pissarro and Julie buy the Éragny house, and in 1893 Pissarro converted the barn into a studio. In old age a recurring eye infection kept him from working outdoors except in warm weather, so he painted from hotel windows in Rouen, Paris, Le Havre, Dieppe and London. He died in Paris on 13 November 1903, aged 73, of sepsis, and was buried in Père Lachaise Cemetery. The art historian Diane Kelder wrote that no member of the Impressionist group did more to mediate the disputes that threatened to break it apart. Cézanne said that Pissarro had been a father for him.
camille-saint-saens: Saint-Saëns was born in Paris, the only child of Jacques-Joseph-Victor Saint-Saëns, an official in the French Ministry of the Interior, and Françoise-Clémence, née Collin. Less than two months after the christening his father died of consumption. The boy was taken to the country for his health and lived for two years with a nurse at Corbeil, 29 kilometres south of Paris. He always considered himself a true Parisian.

On leaving the Conservatoire in 1853, Saint-Saëns became organist at Saint-Merri, where weddings and funerals gave him a comfortable income and spare time to compose. In 1861 he took his only teaching post, at the École Niedermeyer, in charge of piano studies. He scandalised some austere colleagues by introducing his students to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, and Gabriel Fauré remembered the lessons with lasting gratitude.

In 1870, with Romain Bussine, he discussed a society to promote new French music. He served in the National Guard in the Franco-Prussian War. The Société Nationale de Musique, with the motto Ars Gallica, was founded in February 1871, with Bussine as president and Saint-Saëns as vice-president. He was elected to the Institut de France in 1881, and in 1906 and 1909 he made successful tours of the United States as pianist and conductor.

Saint-Saëns was the first major French composer to write piano concertos. The Second, in G minor (1868), became one of his most popular works, and the pianist Zygmunt Stojowski said it begins like Bach and ends like Offenbach. The Fifth, the Egyptian concerto of 1896, was written while he was wintering in Luxor. His Third Symphony has prominent parts for piano and organ and is dedicated to the memory of Liszt.

He wrote twelve operas. Henry VIII became a repertory piece in his lifetime, but since his death only Samson et Dalila has been regularly staged. He composed more than 140 mélodies and set Victor Hugo most often. Committed to the structures of earlier French composers, he came into conflict in later years with the impressionist and expressionist schools.
camillo-benso-count-of-cavour: Camillo Benso was born in Turin on 10 August 1810, during Napoleonic rule, into a family that had acquired estates during the French occupation. His godparents were Napoleon's sister Pauline and her husband, Prince Camillo Borghese. He joined the Engineer Corps of the Royal Sardinian Army in 1827. Reading Jeremy Bentham and Benjamin Constant made him a liberal and a suspect to the police, and he resigned his commission in November 1831. He managed the family estate at Grinzane and served as its mayor until 1848, held that economic progress had to come before political change, and backed railways and canals.

The Revolutions of 1848 let him enter politics, and he founded the newspaper Il Risorgimento. After the Piedmontese defeat at Novara and the abdication of Charles Albert in favour of Victor Emmanuel II, he became minister of agriculture, commerce and the navy in 1850 and of finance in 1851. His railway programme gave Piedmont 800 kilometres of track by 1860. With Urbano Rattazzi he formed a coalition that brought down Massimo d'Azeglio's cabinet in November 1852, and he became prime minister. His methods included heavy use of emergency powers and rigging elections, and the national debt rose sixfold. Piedmont joined the Crimean War on 10 January 1855, which earned it a place at the Congress of Paris.

At Plombières in July 1858 Cavour agreed with Napoleon III that France would help Piedmont fight Austria in return for Savoy and Nice. After Magenta and Solferino Napoleon signed the Armistice of Villafranca on 11 July 1859, and Cavour resigned in fury. Recalled on 20 January 1860, he ceded Savoy and Nice to France to annex Tuscany and Emilia. Garibaldi's thousand volunteers landed at Marsala on 11 May 1860 and conquered Sicily and then Naples. Cavour invaded Umbria and Marche to stop them marching on Rome, and Garibaldi handed the south to the king.

In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II declared the Kingdom of Italy and Cavour became its first prime minister. He held that Rome should be the seat of a free church in a free state. Exhausted, he fell ill, presumably with malaria, and was bled several times. He died on 6 June 1861 and was buried at Santena. Venice joined Italy in 1866 and Rome in 1870. Cavour had at first aimed to expand Piedmont rather than to unite Italy, but by his death the state was five times its earlier size and ranked among Europe's great powers.
campeche: Campeche lies in southeast Mexico, bordered by Tabasco, Yucatán and Quintana Roo, by the Petén department of Guatemala to the south and the Orange Walk District of Belize, with 523 kilometres of shoreline on the Gulf of Mexico. The name derives from Can Pech, the Maya name of a chiefdom of the southwestern Yucatán Peninsula at the time the Spanish arrived; its capital, Ah-Kin-Pech, stood where the city of Campeche is now. The native name means place of snakes and ticks.

The Maya were the first people to dominate the area, and their main cities were Edzná, Xtampak and later Calakmul and Becán. The civilization reached its height between 600 and 900 CE, and from about 1000 the cities were abandoned for unknown reasons. In 1517 Francisco Hernández de Córdoba and Antón de Alaminos landed at Can-Pech and renamed it San Lázaro. At Champotón Hernández de Córdoba was attacked and died of his wounds, so the Spanish called the bay the Bay of the Bad Fight. The conquest of the peninsula began in earnest in 1540 under Francisco de Montejo, father and son, and the capital was founded that year.

The city was a rich port during the colonial period and suffered more than 21 major pirate attacks. After the sack of 1685 by English and French buccaneers, who plundered the surroundings for two months, fortifications were begun that took 24 years to complete: a wall with four main gates, three to the land and one to the sea, and forts including San Carlos, Santa Rosa, San Juan and San Francisco. Only one pirate, Barbillas, found a way in, in 1708. After Mexican independence the city declined, and Campeche split from the province of Yucatán in the mid-19th century, mostly because of political friction with Mérida.

Campeche is one of the 31 states that, with Mexico City, make up the 32 federal entities of Mexico, and has thirteen municipalities. Much of its territory is filled with archaeological sites, almost all Maya, among them Calakmul, Edzná, Becán, Chicanná and Río Bec. The Calakmul Biosphere Reserve was created in 1989. The historic buildings of the capital, formally San Francisco de Campeche, are protected by decree.
canaan: Canaan was an ancient Semitic-speaking civilization and region of the southern Levant in the late 2nd millennium BCE. Egyptian texts of that millennium use the name for an Egyptian-ruled colony whose boundaries broadly match those of the Hebrew Bible: the Mediterranean Sea to the west, the vicinity of Hamath in Syria to the north, the Jordan Valley to the east and a line from the Dead Sea to around Gaza to the south. The Egyptians also called the Levantine coast Retjenu, and the region between Ascalon and the Lebanon, inland to the Sea of Galilee, Djahy.

The name appears as Kinâḫna in the Amarna letters of the 14th century BCE. Its origin is uncertain; one early explanation derives it from a Semitic root meaning to be low or subjugated. The Akkadian word kinahhu referred to purple-dyed wool, a key export, and the Greeks may have taken the name Phoenikes for the Canaanites from their word for crimson or purple.

Scholars use several periodizations. Metalworking Ghassulian settlers entered Canaan around 4500 BCE, at the start of the Chalcolithic. In the Early Bronze Age Ebla was incorporated by about 2300 BCE into the Akkadian Empire of Sargon the Great and Naram-Sin. In the Middle Bronze Age, from 2000 to 1550 BCE, urbanism returned and the region was divided among small city-states, of which Hazor seems to have been the most important, within a wide international trading network.

In the early Late Bronze Age, Canaanite confederacies centred on Megiddo and Kadesh were fully brought into the Egyptian and Hittite empires. By the Early Iron Age the southern Levant was dominated by the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, the Philistine city-states, and Moab, Ammon, Aram-Damascus and Edom. The Neo-Assyrian Empire conquered the whole region in the 10th and 9th centuries BCE and held it for three hundred years.

The name Canaanites is attested many centuries later as the endonym of the people the Greeks called Phoenicians from about 500 BCE, and the Punics of North Africa used a form of it of themselves. In the Hebrew Bible Canaan and the Canaanites appear some 160 times, and Canaan is the land of the Promised Land. The biblical scholar Mark Smith, citing archaeology, holds that Israelite culture largely overlapped with and derived from Canaanite culture.
canada: Canada is the second-largest country by total area, encompassing 9,984,670 square kilometres, and has the world's longest coastline, of 243,042 kilometres. It shares the world's largest land border with the United States, spanning 8,891 kilometres. The country has seven physiographic regions, among them the Canadian Shield, the Interior Plains and the Western Cordillera. It has over 2,000,000 lakes, and boreal forests prevail throughout. Canadian Forces Station Alert, on the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, is the world's northernmost settlement.

Indigenous peoples have continuously inhabited what is now Canada for thousands of years, and they include the First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Their population at the time of the first European settlements is estimated at between 200,000 and 2 million, and it declined by 40 to 80 percent as a consequence of colonization, through European diseases, conflicts over the fur trade, conflicts with colonial authorities and settlers, and the loss of land.

British and French expeditions explored and later settled along the Atlantic coast from the 16th century, and France ceded nearly all of its colonies in North America in 1763. Early interactions were relatively peaceful, but friendship and peace treaties gave way to the dispossession of Indigenous lands.

Canada was formed in 1867 through Confederation as a federal dominion of four provinces. Settler colonialism peaked in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the government funded Indian residential schools administered by Christian churches. These are considered part of a genocide of Indigenous peoples because of their forced assimilation and the large-scale removal of children from their families. A reconciliation commission was formed in 2008. Autonomy from the United Kingdom grew through the Statute of Westminster, 1931, and the Canada Act 1982 severed the remaining legal dependence.

Canada has ten provinces and three territories, with Ottawa as the capital and Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver as the three largest metropolitan areas. It is a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy, and it is officially bilingual in English and French in the federal jurisdiction. The 2021 census enumerated 36,991,981 people, and the population is estimated to have passed 40,000,000 in 2023. About 80 percent live within 150 kilometres of the border with the contiguous United States. Multiculturalism is official state policy.
canary-islands: The Canary Islands are an archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean, about 100 kilometres off the northwest coast of Africa. The seven main islands, from largest to smallest by area, are Tenerife, Fuerteventura, Gran Canaria, Lanzarote, La Palma, La Gomera and El Hierro. All are volcanic in origin, and with the Azores, Cape Verde, Madeira and the Savage Isles they form the Macaronesia ecoregion. Historically the chain was called the Fortunate Isles.

The western islands, El Hierro, La Palma and La Gomera, are influenced by the moist Canary Current and carry extensive subtropical laurisilva forest, while Fuerteventura and Lanzarote, nearest to Africa, are effectively desert or semi-desert. Mount Teide on Tenerife is the highest peak in Spain.

Linguistic, genetic and archaeological analyses indicate that indigenous peoples were living on the islands at least 2,000 years ago, possibly 3,000, and shared a common origin with the Amazighs of the nearby North African coast. They may have reached the islands in several small boats, landing first on Lanzarote and Fuerteventura. They came to be known collectively as the Guanches, although that name had belonged only to the indigenous inhabitants of Tenerife.

According to a 2024 study by the University of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, archaeological evidence shows that the Romans were the first to establish contact, between the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE. During the Age of Sail the islands were the main stopover for Spanish galleons on the way to the Americas, which sailed that far south to catch the prevailing northeasterly trade winds.

The archipelago is the southernmost autonomous community of Spain, established in 1982. It has two provinces, Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas, created by splitting the Province of Canary Islands in 1927, and the cities of Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas de Gran Canaria are joint capitals.

The name Islas Canarias probably derives from the Latin Canariae Insulae, meaning Islands of the Dogs, from Pliny the Elder's account of vast multitudes of very large dogs on Canaria. The canary bird takes its name from the islands. San Cristóbal de La Laguna on Tenerife is a World Heritage Site, as is Mount Teide.
canberra: Canberra lies near the Brindabella Ranges, part of the Australian Alps, about 150 km inland from Australia's east coast. Its urban area has an elevation of about 580 m, and the highest point near it is Mount Majura at 888 m. The Molonglo River was dammed to form Lake Burley Griffin, and it then flows into the Murrumbidgee. The area was a flood plain before the lake was filled.

The name derives from the Ngunnawal language of a local clan that the first British colonists called the Canberry, Kanberri or Nganbra tribe. Joshua John Moore, the first European landowner in the region, named his grant Canberry in 1823. The form Canberra began to appear around 1857. Suggested meanings include meeting place.

The first peoples of the area include the Ngunnawal and Ngambri. Archaeological evidence suggests human activity there 21,000 years ago. The Canberry or Nganbra clan lived mostly around Sullivan's Creek and had ceremonial grounds at the base of Galambary (Black Mountain), while the Pialligo clan had land around what is now Canberra Airport. The people managed the land with fire, farmed yams and hunted. Galambary was a meeting and business site, mainly for men, and an initiation site.

European settlement began in the first half of the 19th century. The federation of the Australian colonies was achieved on 1 January 1901, and the new capital was founded and formally named Canberra in 1913, as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne. It is an entirely planned city, based on a design by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, influenced by the garden city movement and aligned with landmarks such as Black Mountain, Mount Ainslie and Capital Hill.

Canberra is the capital of Australia and the largest population centre in the Australian Capital Territory, with an estimated 484,630 people. It is the country's largest inland city. It is the seat of the federal government, with Parliament House, Government House and the High Court, and it hosts all foreign embassies in Australia.

Among its national institutions are the Australian War Memorial, the Australian National University, established in 1946, the National Gallery, the National Museum and the National Library. The Royal Military College Duntroon is also there, and Floriade is the largest flower festival in the Southern Hemisphere.
cannon: The word cannon derives from the Old Italian cannone, meaning large tube, from the Latin canna and the Greek kanna, reed. It has referred to a gun since 1326 in Italy and 1418 in England. The earliest known depiction of cannons may appear in Song dynasty China as early as the 12th century, but solid evidence does not appear until the 13th century. The cannon was probably a parallel development or evolution of the fire lance, a short-range weapon combining a gunpowder-filled tube and a polearm, whose paper and bamboo barrels were eventually replaced by metal.

Elsewhere the dates are less settled. There is no clear consensus on when the cannon first appeared in the Islamic world, with dates ranging from 1260 to the mid-14th century. Documentary evidence of cannons in Russia does not appear until 1382, and Ivan III established the first Russian cannon foundry in Moscow in 1475. Cannons reached the Javanese Majapahit Empire when a Mongol-Chinese army under Ike Mese invaded Java in 1293.

A cannon has the form of a truncated cone with an internal cylindrical bore that holds the charge and the projectile. The thickest and strongest part lies near the charge, which is ignited through a thin tube called the vent. The main body is divided into the chase, the reinforce and the cascabel, and a cannon's calibre is determined by the diameter of its bore. By the 16th century cannons were made in great variety, and the general rule was that the longer the barrel, the longer the range.

Cannons were used primarily as anti-infantry weapons until around 1374, when large cannons were recorded breaching walls for the first time in Europe. In 1464 the Ottoman Empire cast the Great Turkish Bombard, which weighed 16,000 kilograms. Larger guns forced engineers to build stronger castle walls, and in India the fort of Raicher had gun ports built into its walls for defensive cannons. Field artillery became more important after the introduction of the limber, which greatly improved mobility.

In the 1770s a cannon was manned by two gunners, six soldiers and four officers of artillery. The bore was cleaned with a wet sponge, powder was added, then wadding and the ball, which was rammed down; at 45 degrees the ball had its utmost range. Decoys also had a use: the Quaker gun, a painted log, was used by Colonel William Washington's Continental Army in 1780, when about 100 Loyalists surrendered rather than face bombardment.
canterbury: Canterbury lies on the River Stour, not far from its mouth on the Strait of Dover, in east Kent. The site has been occupied since prehistoric times. The Roman name Durovernum Cantiacorum means Durovernum of the Cantiaci, and replaced an earlier British name reconstructed as Durouernon, meaning stronghold by the alder grove. In Sub-Roman Britain it was Cair Ceint, the stronghold of Kent, and the Jutes who occupied it called it Cantwareburh in Old English.

Canterbury was first recorded as the main settlement of the Cantiaci. In the 1st century CE the Romans captured it and rebuilt it with a grid of streets, a theatre, a temple, a forum and public baths. They kept no major garrison, but its position on Watling Street, in relation to the ports of Richborough, Dover and Lymne, gave it strategic importance. In the late 3rd century they built an earth bank and a wall with seven gates round it. It later served as capital of the Jute kingdom of Kent.

A large Viking army besieged Canterbury in 1011, and the city was pillaged. Remembering the destruction caused by the Danes, its inhabitants did not resist William the Conqueror in 1066, and William ordered a wooden castle built beside the Roman wall, rebuilt in stone in the early 12th century. In the mid-16th century Canterbury hosted the first congregation of Huguenot refugees in England, founded around 1548 and scattered in 1553–4 under Mary I. In 1647, during the English Civil War, the Plum Pudding Riots broke out, and the trial of the rioters led to a Kentish revolt.

Canterbury is a World Heritage Site and its cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury. Its surviving past includes a city wall founded in Roman times and rebuilt in the 14th century, the Westgate Towers, the ruins of St Augustine's Abbey and the Norman castle. The Canterbury and Whitstable Railway, which ran from 1830 to 1953, was the first regular passenger steam railway in the world. The city's economy rests on tourism, higher education and retail.
cape-horn: Cape Horn lies on Hornos Island in the Hermite Islands group, at the southern end of the Tierra del Fuego archipelago in southern Chile, at about 56 degrees south. It is not the most southerly point of South America, which is Águila Islet, but it marks the northern boundary of the Drake Passage, the strait between South America and Antarctica, and the place where the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans meet. The cape lies in Chilean territorial waters, within Cabo de Hornos National Park, and the Chilean Navy maintains a station on the island with a residence, chapel and lighthouse.

The Dutchmen Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire first rounded the cape in 1616 and named it Kaap Hoorn after the city of Hoorn in the Netherlands. The Strait of Magellan, between the mainland and Tierra del Fuego, had been used for trade well before the Horn was discovered, but is narrow, and for decades Cape Horn was a major milestone on the clipper route by which sailing ships carried trade around the world. The need to round it was greatly reduced by the opening of the Panama Canal in August 1914.

The passage is regarded as perhaps the most dangerous ship route in the world, and many ships have been wrecked and many sailors have died attempting it. Winds in these latitudes blow from west to east almost uninterrupted by land, and the Andes and the Antarctic Peninsula funnel them into the narrow Drake Passage. The waves become shorter and steeper over the shallow water south of the Horn, and rogue waves of up to 30 metres are reported west of it. Icebergs are a further hazard. Passage from east to west, against the winds and currents, was a particular problem for traditional sailing ships.

There are no regular commercial routes around the Horn, although cruise ships and vessels bound for the Antarctic Peninsula pass it. Rounding the Horn remains one of the major challenges in yachting. A memorial near the station, a sculpture by José Balcells of the silhouette of an albatross, was erected in 1992 in remembrance of the sailors who died attempting to round the Horn. The cape belongs to the commune of Cabo de Hornos, whose capital is Puerto Williams.
cape-of-good-hope: The Cape of Good Hope is a rocky headland on the Atlantic coast of the Cape Peninsula in South Africa, about 2.3 kilometres west and a little north of Cape Point. It is a common misconception that it is the southern tip of Africa; the southernmost point is Cape Agulhas, about 150 kilometres to the east-southeast. Following the western African coastline from the equator, however, the Cape of Good Hope marks the point where a ship begins to travel more eastward than southward. Cape Town lies about 50 kilometres to the north, in Table Bay.

Herodotus records that around 600 BCE Necho II reputedly commissioned Phoenicians to sail from the Red Sea around Africa to the mouth of the Nile, which would be the first completion of the Cape Route. The account came to him by oral tradition. Eudoxus of Cyzicus, a Greek navigator for Ptolemy VIII, found in about 116 BCE the wreck of a ship that appeared to have come from Gades, and concluded that it had sailed round Africa; his own later attempt failed and his fate is unknown. The Fra Mauro map of 1450 depicts the Indian Ocean as connected to the Atlantic and records a voyage by an Indian junk around 1420.

The first European to reach the cape was the Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias, who named it the Cape of Storms, Cabo das Tormentas. John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope because of the optimism the opening of a sea route to India and the East engendered. The Khoikhoi lived in the area when the Dutch first settled in 1652. On 6 April of that year Jan van Riebeeck established a resupply camp for the Dutch East India Company in Table Bay, which developed into Cape Town and became known as the Tavern of the Seas. On 31 December 1687 a community of Huguenots arrived from the Netherlands, since the Company needed skilled farmers.

British troops occupied the Cape Colony in 1795, after the Dutch Republic was occupied by France, and again on 19 January 1806 following the Battle of Blaauwberg. The colony existed from 1795 to 1802 and again from 1806 to 1910. Today the cape is a section of Table Mountain National Park, with fynbos vegetation that belongs to the Cape Floristic Kingdom, and at least 250 bird species, including a mainland colony of African penguins. In legend it is the home of the Flying Dutchman, and the poet Luís de Camões invented the giant Adamastor in Os Lusíadas, first printed in 1572, as a symbol of the dangers of rounding the Cape of Storms.
cape-town: Cape Town stands on the shore of Table Bay, at a latitude of about 33.55 degrees south. Table Mountain, with near vertical cliffs and a flat summit more than 1,000 metres high, forms a mountainous backdrop with Devil's Peak and Lion's Head on either side and creates the City Bowl, which holds the central business district. To the south the Cape Peninsula runs 40 kilometres into the Atlantic Ocean and ends at Cape Point, and many suburbs lie on the Cape Flats, a plain that joins the peninsula to the mainland. Robben Island in Table Bay is part of the city, and Table Mountain National Park lies within its boundaries.

The earliest known remains of human occupation in the region were found at Peers Cave in Fish Hoek in the late 1920s; earlier estimates of an upper Pleistocene origin have since been revised to the mid-Holocene. Bartolomeu Dias, the first European to reach the area, arrived in 1488 and named it the Cape of Storms. John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope, because the opening of a sea route to India raised such optimism, and Vasco da Gama recorded sighting it in 1497. In 1510, at the Battle of Salt River, the Portuguese admiral Francisco de Almeida and sixty-four of his men were killed by the Khoikhoi Goringhaiqua, who used cattle trained to respond to whistles and shouts.

Ships of several nations, mainly Portuguese, regularly stopped in Table Bay in the late sixteenth century on the way to the Indies. They traded tobacco, copper and iron with the Khoikhoi clans of the region for fresh meat and other provisions. In 1652 Jan van Riebeeck and other employees of the United East India Company were sent to establish a way-station for ships travelling to the Dutch East Indies, and they built the Fort de Goede Hoop, later replaced by the Castle of Good Hope.

The settlement grew slowly because adequate labour was hard to find. The shortage led the local authorities to import enslaved people from Indonesia and Madagascar, many of whom are ancestors of the present Cape Coloured and Cape Malay communities.

Cape Town is the legislative capital of South Africa, the seat of its Parliament, and the capital of the Western Cape. It is the country's oldest city. It has the highest density of Cape Dutch buildings in the world, a style that combines the architectural traditions of the Netherlands, Germany, France and Indonesia. Mostert's Mill in Mowbray, built in 1796, is the only complete windmill in South Africa. The Cape Floristic Region, including Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.
cape-verde: Cape Verde is a horseshoe-shaped cluster of ten volcanic islands, nine of them inhabited, and eight islets, with a land area of about 4,033 square kilometres. They lie between 600 and 850 km west of Cap-Vert on the Senegalese coast, from which the country takes its name. Cap-Vert comes from the Portuguese Cabo Verde, meaning green cape, a name Portuguese explorers gave to the headland in 1444. The islands are divided into the Barlavento or windward group in the north and the Sotavento or leeward group in the south. Santiago is the largest and holds the capital, Praia.

The islands were uninhabited before the arrival of Europeans. Genoese and Portuguese navigators found them around 1456. Portuguese records credit the first discoveries to António de Noli, born in Genoa, who was later appointed governor by King Afonso V. In 1462 Portuguese settlers founded Ribeira Grande on Santiago, today called Cidade Velha, the first permanent European settlement in the tropics.

In the 16th century the islands prospered from the Atlantic slave trade. The English privateer Francis Drake sacked Ribeira Grande twice in 1585, when it was part of the Iberian Union, and after a French attack in 1712 the town declined relative to Praia, which became the capital in 1770. The decline of the slave trade in the 19th century brought economic crisis, but the islands' position on mid-Atlantic shipping lanes made them a good place to resupply ships, and the harbour of Mindelo grew into a commercial centre. In 1951 Portugal changed the status of Cape Verde from a colony to an overseas province in an attempt to blunt nationalism. The country became independent in 1975.

Cape Verde is a unitary semi-presidential republic whose constitution was adopted in 1980 and revised in 1992, 1995 and 1999. Praia is the capital and largest city. Portuguese is the official language, and Cape Verdean Creole, called Kriolu, is the mother tongue of virtually all Cape Verdeans. The people descend from Africans, free or enslaved, and Europeans of various origins, and the diaspora outnumbers the people on the islands.
capitalism: Capitalism in its modern form is traced to agrarian capitalism and mercantilism in the early Renaissance, in city-states such as Florence. Capital had existed on a small scale for centuries in merchant, renting and lending activities. During the Islamic Golden Age, Arabs promulgated policies such as free trade and banking, and their use of Indo-Arabic numerals facilitated bookkeeping; these innovations reached Europe through Venice and Pisa.

In 16th-century England the manorial system broke down, land became concentrated in fewer landlords and workers were increasingly employed in a money-based economy instead of as serfs. From the 16th to the 18th centuries mercantilism prevailed, a system of trade for profit, though goods were still largely produced by non-capitalist methods. Most scholars see it as the origin of the modern system, but Karl Polanyi held that capitalism required generalised markets for land, labour and money, and so could not be said to exist before 1834, when a competitive labour market was established in England.

Capitalism is an economic system based on private ownership of the means of production and its use to obtain profit. Its elements include private property, the profit motive, capital accumulation, competitive markets and wage labour. Its forms, among them laissez-faire, state and welfare capitalism, differ in their degree of free markets, public ownership and regulation. There is no universally agreed definition.

The term capitalist, meaning an owner of capital, dates to the mid-17th century. Louis Blanc in 1850 and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon in 1861 are credited with the first modern use of capitalism, and Karl Marx wrote of the capitalist mode of production in Das Kapital (1867). Because socialist critics coined the word, Robert Hessen called it a term of disparagement.

The Industrial Revolution of the 18th century made capitalism the dominant mode of production, characterised by factory work and a complex division of labour. It spread across the world in the 19th and 20th centuries. In the 19th century it was largely unregulated; after World War II it became more regulated through Keynesianism, followed from the 1980s by a return of less regulated capitalism termed neoliberalism.
caracalla: Caracalla was born Lucius Septimius Bassianus at Lugdunum in Gaul, the elder son of Septimius Severus and Julia Domna. At seven he was renamed Marcus Aurelius Antoninus as part of his father's attempt at union with the families of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius.

His father, acclaimed Augustus in 193, had himself adopted posthumously by Marcus Aurelius, and Caracalla was made Caesar in 195 or 196. On 28 January 198, aged nine, he became joint Augustus, on the day of his father's triumph over the Parthian Empire, and in 202 he was consul with his father.

Severus died at Eboracum on 4 February 211 while on campaign in Caledonia, leaving Caracalla and his brother Geta as joint rulers. On 26 December 211, at a reconciliation meeting arranged by their mother, Geta was killed by Praetorian Guards loyal to Caracalla, and it is widely accepted that Caracalla ordered it. He persecuted Geta's supporters, and the Senate pronounced a damnatio memoriae on Geta, whose name it became a capital offence to speak or write; an estimated 20,000 people were massacred. Julia Domna took on more of the government, since Caracalla found administration mundane.

In 212 he issued the Constitutio Antoniniana, granting full Roman citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire except the dediticii. In 213 he left Rome, never to return, and campaigned against the Alamanni on the German frontier, defeating some tribes and settling others by diplomacy. In December 215 he slaughtered a deputation of leading citizens at Alexandria after the city mocked his claim to have killed Geta in self-defence, and set his troops loose on the city for several days of looting.
He raised the annual pay of a legionary from 2,000 sesterces to 2,700 to 3,000, and the cost led him to debase the coinage. In 215 he introduced the antoninianus, intended as a double denarius.

In 216 Caracalla began a campaign against the Parthians after King Artabanus IV refused a marriage proposal. On 8 April 217, travelling from Edessa to Carrhae to visit a temple of the moon god Sin, he was stabbed by a Roman soldier, Justin Martialis, and the two Praetorian tribunes completed the killing. Macrinus succeeded him three days later, and had him deified.

Cassius Dio, Herodian and the Historia Augusta portray him as a cruel tyrant and a soldier first and an emperor second, a view that has largely persisted. The Constitutio Antoniniana goes almost unnoticed in the classical records. In the late 18th century French painters revived his image, as the tyranny ascribed to him seemed to parallel that ascribed to Louis XVI.
caracas: Caracas lies along the Guaire River in the Caracas Valley of the Venezuelan Central Range, a small and irregular valley close to the Caribbean Sea. A steep range, Cerro El Ávila, rises 2,200 metres between the valley and the shore, and about 15 kilometres of El Ávila National Park separate the city from the coast. The valley floor lies between 870 and 1,043 metres above sea level, and the historic centre stands at about 900 metres. The highest point of the Capital District, Pico El Ávila, reaches 2,159 metres.

The Guaire crosses the city and empties into the Tuy River. The city is occasionally struck by earthquakes, notably in 1641, 1812 and 1967. The region was formed in the Late Cretaceous, and the city sits mostly on metamorphic rock.

Before the city was founded in 1567, the valley was populated by indigenous peoples. Francisco Fajardo, the son of a Spanish captain and a Waikeri cacique, began establishing settlements around La Guaira and the Caracas valley between 1555 and 1560. His plantation of 1562 did not last, as natives of the region led by Terepaima and Guaicaipuro destroyed it, as they had destroyed the Villa de San Francisco founded by Juan Rodríguez de Suárez in 1561.

The settlers who eventually founded Caracas came from Coro, the capital of the German colony of Klein-Venedig, which Spaniards had controlled in practice from the 1540s. Moving eastward, they founded inland towns including Barquisimeto and Valencia before reaching the valley. In 1591 Simón de Bolívar, an ancestor of the liberator Simón Bolívar, petitioned King Philip II for a coat of arms. The king granted it by Royal Cedula on 4 September 1591 and declared Caracas The Most Noble and Very Loyal City of Santiago de León de Caracas.

Caracas is the capital and largest city of Venezuela and the centre of a metropolitan region estimated at over 5 million people. Its historic centre is the Caracas Cathedral on Bolívar Square. The Central University of Venezuela, founded in 1721, is the oldest university in the country, and its campus, designed by the architect Carlos Raúl Villanueva, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

In the 1940s and 1950s, after the Second World War, a wave of European immigrants, mainly Spanish, Italian and Portuguese, settled in the country, and the city has been shaped by many ethnic and cultural groups. The Caracas Metro has operated since 27 March 1983.
carcassonne: Carcassonne lies in the plain of the Aude, about 80 kilometres east of Toulouse, between the historic trade routes linking the Atlantic to the Mediterranean Sea and the Massif Central to the Pyrénées. Settlement there dates to about 3500 BCE. The hill site of Carsac, a Celtic place-name, became an important trading place in the 6th century BCE, when the Volcae Tectosages fortified it as an oppidum. The popular story of a lady named Carcas and the ringing of bells is a modern reconstruction of a 16th-century depiction.

The Romans fortified the hilltop around 100 BCE and made it a colonia; the lower courses of the northern ramparts date from Gallo-Roman times. In 462 the Romans officially ceded Septimania to the Visigothic king Theodoric II, who had held Carcassonne since 453. The first count known by name is Bello, of the time of Charlemagne, who founded the Bellonid dynasty. In 1067 the county passed to Raimond-Bernard Trencavel through his marriage with Ermengard, sister of the last count.

In August 1209 the crusading army of the Papal Legate, the abbot Arnaud Amalric, besieged the city, a stronghold of Occitan Cathars. Viscount Raymond-Roger de Trencavel was imprisoned while negotiating its surrender and died in mysterious circumstances three months later. The people were allowed to leave with nothing but the shirts on their backs, and Simon de Montfort became the new viscount and added to the fortifications. The city submitted to France in 1247 and became a border fortress against the Crown of Aragon under the 1258 Treaty of Corbeil. Edward the Black Prince failed to take it in 1355, though his troops destroyed the lower town.

The Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 moved the border away and reduced Carcassonne's military importance. A decree of 1849 ordered the decayed fortress demolished, but a campaign led by the mayor Jean-Pierre Cros-Mayrevieille and the writer Prosper Mérimée saved it, and Eugène Viollet-le-Duc restored it from 1853 until his death in 1879. His slate roofs and pointed tips, more typical of northern France, were criticised in his lifetime. The citadel was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1997, and Carcassonne is the prefecture of the Aude.
cardiff: Cardiff is the county town of the historic county of Glamorgan. The centre of the city is relatively flat and bounded by hills to the east, north and west, and the River Taff flows past Cardiff Castle. The highest point in the local authority area is Garth Hill, at 307 m. The position, with easy access to the coalfields of the South Wales Valleys, influenced the city's development as the world's largest coal port. The Welsh name, Caerdydd, derives from Middle Welsh Caerdyf, meaning the fort of the Taff, the fort probably being the one the Romans established.

People had settled in the area by about 6000 BCE, in the early Neolithic, and burial chambers such as Tinkinswood and St Lythans lie a few miles to the west. Four Iron Age hill forts and enclosures have been identified within the county boundary, among them Caerau Hillfort, which encloses 5.1 hectares. Cardiff Castle has stood at the heart of the city since the Norman period, within the walls of the old Roman fort. Welsh was the majority language from the 13th century until the Victorian growth of the city; as late as 1850, five of the twelve Anglican churches within the present boundaries held services only in Welsh.

In 1536 the Laws in Wales Acts made Glamorganshire and Cardiff its county town, and in 1538 Henry VIII closed the Dominican and Franciscan friaries. John Crichton-Stuart, 2nd Marquess of Bute, born in 1793, spent his life building the Cardiff docks and was later called the creator of modern Cardiff. A boat service to Bristol opened in 1815. Dic Penderyn was tried and hanged in 1831, after unrest that followed the Napoleonic Wars. Cardiff became a county borough on 1 April 1889, with more than 123,000 people.

Edward VII granted Cardiff city status on 28 October 1905, and in 1955 it was proclaimed capital of Wales. National institutions followed, including the National Museum of Wales and the Welsh National War Memorial, though the National Library of Wales went elsewhere, partly because its founder, Sir John Williams, thought Cardiff had a non-Welsh population. Since 1922 the city has included Llandaff, with its cathedral. The Senedd, the Welsh Parliament, has sat in Cardiff Bay since 1999, when it was founded as the National Assembly for Wales, and its building opened on 1 March 2006. The 2021 census counted 362,400 people in the city.
cardinal-richelieu: Armand du Plessis was born in Paris on 9 September 1585, the fourth of five children, and was delicate from childhood. His family belonged to the lesser nobility of Poitou; his father, François du Plessis, seigneur de Richelieu, was a soldier and courtier who died of fever in the French Wars of Religion when Armand was five. In 1606 Henry IV nominated him to the Bishopric of Luçon, which the family held. Since he was below the canonical minimum age, he travelled to Rome for a dispensation from Pope Paul V and was consecrated bishop in April 1607. On his return he was heralded as a reformer and became the first bishop in France to implement the reforms of the Council of Trent.

In 1614 Richelieu represented the clergy of Poitou at the Estates-General. He rose by serving the queen mother Marie de' Medici's favourite, Concino Concini, and in 1616 was made Secretary of State with responsibility for foreign affairs. He became a cardinal in 1622 and Louis XIII's principal minister in 1624. His policy had two aims: to centralize power in France and to oppose the Habsburg dynasty, which ruled in Austria and Spain. In 1626 he abolished the position of Constable of France and ordered all fortified castles razed, except those needed against invaders, which made him hated by most of the nobility. In 1627 he personally commanded the troops besieging the Huguenot stronghold of La Rochelle.

Abroad he subsidized the Dutch Republic against Spain, and in 1629, alarmed by Emperor Ferdinand II's growing influence, he gave money to incite Sweden to intervene in Germany. He encouraged Louis XIII to colonize the Americas through the Company of New France, and the Ordonnance of 1627 deemed Indians who converted to Catholicism natural Frenchmen. He also renovated the Sorbonne and patronised the arts.

Near the end of his life Richelieu faced a plot by the marquis de Cinq-Mars, whom he had introduced at court. He suffered from recurrent fevers, intestinal tuberculosis and migraine, and he died on 4 December 1642, naming Jules Mazarin as his successor. He left his library, with some 900 manuscripts, to be open to scholars. Historians credit him with replacing a largely feudal political structure with centralized power, work that Louis XIV continued. He is also noted for authoritarian measures: he censored the press, kept a network of spies and had those who conspired against him prosecuted and executed.
caribbean: The Caribbean is a region of thousands of islands, islets, reefs and cays centred on the Caribbean Sea and lying largely on the Caribbean plate. Island arcs mark its northern and eastern edges: the Greater Antilles, including Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico, in the north, and the Lesser Antilles in the east and south. The Bahamas, the Turks and Caicos Islands and Barbados are counted as part of the region though they do not border the sea. The term West Indies is often used interchangeably with the Caribbean. The region takes its name from the Caribs, after whom Spanish colonists named it.

The oldest evidence of human presence is at Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad, where remains about 7,000 years old have been found. Consistent dates of 3100 BCE appear in Cuba and of 2000 BCE in Antigua. At the time of European contact the dominant groups were the Taíno of the Greater Antilles and the Island Caribs of the southern Lesser Antilles, and the population is estimated to have been about 750,000.

Christopher Columbus arrived on Hispaniola in 1492. The Spanish assigned enslaved people to conquistadors under the encomienda system, and the Laws of Burgos of 1512 were meant to protect the rights of the native peoples. Smallpox and measles, to which they had no immunity, and social disruption sharply reduced the Amerindian population, and from 1503 enslaved people from Africa, among them Kongo, Igbo, Akan, Fon and Yoruba, were brought in. England, the Netherlands and France sought colonies of their own, and colonial rivalries made the region a battleground of European wars for centuries. Spain ceded Jamaica to England, while Martinique and the western third of Hispaniola passed to France.

The principal official languages are Spanish, French, English and Dutch, with Haitian Creole and Papiamento, and almost every country has a creole language or dialect as its everyday speech. Christianity is the main religion, alongside Hinduism, Islam and Rastafari. The islands hold about 8 per cent of the world's coral reefs. In 1973 English-speaking states created the Caribbean Community, CARICOM, in Guyana.
carl-gustaf-emil-mannerheim: Mannerheim was born on 4 June 1867 at Louhisaari Manor in Askainen parish, into a Swedish-speaking aristocratic family. The Mannerheims, originally from Germany as Marhein, became Swedish noblemen in 1693. His great-grandfather, Count Carl Erik Mannerheim, became the first head of the executive of the newly autonomous Grand Duchy of Finland after Sweden lost Finland to the Russian Empire in 1809. His father, heavily in debt, left the family in 1880, and his mother died the following year.

In 1882 he entered the Hamina Cadet School, and in 1889 he was hired as a cornet in a dragoon regiment at Kalisz in Poland. He married Anastasia Arapova in 1892; they had two daughters. He served in the Russo-Japanese War, travelled through Turkestan to Beijing as a secret intelligence officer, and fought on the Austro-Hungarian and Romanian fronts in the First World War, rising to lieutenant general in April 1917.

After Finland declared independence in December 1917, the Senate of Finland faced the socialist Reds in a civil war. On 13 January 1918 Mannerheim was given command of the army of the Whites, about 24,000 mostly untrained men, against some 30,000 Red Guards. At Vaasa he surrounded a Russian garrison of 1,500 to 2,000 men with recruits, only the front rank of them armed, and the garrison surrendered its weapons. The Whites held a victory parade in Helsinki in May.

He was regent from December 1918 to July 1919, won recognition of independence from several Entente powers and ratified the republican constitution although he was a monarchist. He lost the first presidential election to K. J. Ståhlberg in 1919 and held no public office in the interwar years. As chairman of the Defence Council from 1931 he prepared for a possible war with the Soviet Union, and after the Soviet attack of 30 November 1939 he became commander-in-chief at 72, a post he held for five years.

In 1944 the Parliament of Finland unanimously appointed Mannerheim president, and he oversaw peace negotiations with the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom. Finland had made him a field marshal in 1933 and gave him the title Marshal of Finland in 1942, which no one else has held. In poor health, he resigned in March 1946, wrote his memoirs at a sanatorium in Montreux, Switzerland, and died there on 27 January 1951.

Mannerheim is often called the father of modern Finland. According to the historian Tuomas Tepora, a cult of personality grew around him after the civil war, and the Mannerheim Museum in Helsinki memorialises his life.
carl-linnaeus: Carl Linnaeus was born on 23 May 1707 in the village of Råshult in Småland, Sweden, the first child of Nicolaus (Nils) Linnaeus and Christina Brodersonia. His father, a Lutheran minister and amateur botanist, taught him Latin as a small child, and the family moved to the rectory of Stenbrohult when his father became rector there. Linnaeus liked plants from his earliest years, and his father gave him his own patch of land to grow them.

In 1727, at the age of 21, he enrolled at Lund University. Most of his higher education was at Uppsala University, where he began giving lectures in botany in 1730. In May 1732 he set out on an expedition to Lapland, funded by a grant from the Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala, curious about the Sami people.

In April 1735 Linnaeus travelled to the Dutch Republic to study medicine at the University of Harderwijk, and he published the first edition of his Systema Naturae in the Netherlands. After returning to Sweden on 28 June 1738 he worked as a physician at the Admiralty in Stockholm and helped found the Royal Swedish Academy of Science, becoming its first Praeses by drawing of lots. He later became professor of medicine and botany at Uppsala, and in the 1740s he was sent on several journeys through Sweden to find and classify plants and animals.

He taught many students, 17 of whom he called his apostles, and they made botanical expeditions around the world, so that his system spread without his travelling outside Sweden again. He was ennobled in 1761. Illness troubled his last years, and he died on 10 January 1778 in Hammarby.

The first edition of Systema Naturae, printed in 1735, ran to twelve pages. By its 10th edition in 1758 it classified 4,400 species of animals and 7,700 species of plants. Linnaeus's main contribution to taxonomy was the establishment of universally accepted conventions for naming organisms, and his work marks the starting point of the consistent use of binomial nomenclature.

The Linnaean system placed nature in a nested hierarchy of three kingdoms divided into classes, orders, genera and species. His taxonomy of human races has been criticised in the 21st century: some regard him as a forebear of scientific racism, while others hold that his classification was stereotyped but did not imply that any race was superior.
carlos-fuentes: Carlos Fuentes Macías was born in Panama City on 11 November 1928, the son of Berta Macías and Rafael Fuentes, a Mexican diplomat. As the family moved with his father's career, he spent his childhood in several Latin American capitals, an experience he later said gave him the ability to see Latin America as a critical outsider. From 1934 to 1940 his father was posted to the Mexican Embassy in Washington, where he attended an English-language school and began to write. In 1940 the family moved to Santiago, Chile, where his interest in the poetry of Pablo Neruda led him to socialism.

He lived in Mexico for the first time at 16, when he went to study law at the National Autonomous University of Mexico with a diplomatic career in mind, and he later attended the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva.

In 1957 Fuentes became head of cultural relations at the Mexican Secretariat of Foreign Affairs. His first novel, Where the Air Is Clear, appeared in 1958 and made him a national celebrity, allowing him to write full-time. In 1959 he moved to Havana after the Cuban Revolution. He served as Mexico's ambassador to France from 1975 to 1977 and resigned in protest at the appointment of the former president Gustavo Díaz Ordaz as ambassador to Spain. He taught at Cambridge, Princeton, Harvard, Columbia and other universities.

He was long a critic of the Institutional Revolutionary Party government that ruled Mexico from 1929 until 2000. In the 1980s he broke with the poet Octavio Paz over the Sandinistas, and a feud began that lasted until Paz's death in 1998. He received the Miguel de Cervantes Prize and, in 1999, Mexico's highest award, the Belisario Domínguez Medal of Honor. He died on 15 May 2012.

Fuentes named Cervantes, William Faulkner and Balzac as the writers most important to him, and his main theme was Mexican history and identity. Where the Air Is Clear is built around Federico Robles, a former revolutionary turned powerful financier, and presents Mexico City in vignettes. The Death of Artemio Cruz (1962) begins like Citizen Kane with its protagonist on his deathbed and tells his life in flashbacks: a soldier of the Mexican Revolution who becomes wealthy through violence, blackmail and bribery. Fuentes was a leading figure of the Latin American boom of the 1960s and 1970s, with Gabriel García Márquez, Mario Vargas Llosa and Julio Cortázar.

Terra Nostra (1975) tells the story of Hispanic civilisation, moving between the sixteenth and twentieth centuries. The Old Gringo (1985), loosely based on the disappearance of Ambrose Bierce during the Mexican Revolution, became the first United States bestseller by a Mexican author. His work has been translated into 24 languages.
carrara: Carrara is a town in Tuscany on the Carrione River, some 100 kilometres west-northwest of Florence, notable for the white or blue-grey marble quarried there. Its name likely comes from a pre-Roman element, kar, meaning stone, through the Latin carrariae, quarries. Its motto, Fortitudo mea in rota, or My strength is in the wheel, refers to the wheel of the cart that carried marble blocks from the quarry. The Pantheon and Trajan's Column in Rome are built of Carrara marble, and many sculptures of the Renaissance were carved from it.

The Apuan Ligures lived in the region as early as the ninth century BCE. The present town grew from a borough built for workers in the marble quarries that the Romans opened after conquering Liguria in the early second century BCE. In the early Middle Ages it was a Byzantine and then a Lombard possession, and then it fell to the bishops of Luni, to whom Emperor Otto I gave it. It became a city-state in the early 13th century. The bishops regained it in 1230, and their rule ended in 1313, after which it passed to the republics of Pisa, Lucca and Florence, and later to Gian Galeazzo Visconti of Milan.

After the death of Filippo Maria Visconti in 1447 the Malaspina family fought for Carrara, and moved the seat of their lordship there in the second half of the 15th century. Carrara and Massa formed the Duchy of Massa and Carrara, which passed to the Duchy of Modena through the last Malaspina, Maria Teresa, who married Ercole III d'Este. At the end of the 19th century Carrara became the cradle of Italian anarchism, above all among the quarry workers and stone carvers, who led the Lunigiana revolt of January 1894. The Congress of Carrara in 1968 founded the International of Anarchist Federations.

The town lies in the province of Massa and Carrara. Its sights include the 12th-century cathedral and the Ducal Palace, also called the Palazzo Cybo Malaspina, which now houses the Fine Arts Academy and combines a 13th-century castle with a Renaissance palace begun in the late 16th century.
cartography: What counts as the earliest known map is debated, partly because the term map is not well defined and some artifacts that might be maps may be something else. A wall painting that might depict the ancient Anatolian city of Çatalhöyük has been dated to the late 7th millennium BCE, and prehistoric alpine rock carvings at Mount Bego in France and Valcamonica in Italy, dated to the 4th millennium BCE, are widely interpreted as showing cultivated plots.

Other maps of the ancient world include the Minoan House of the Admiral wall painting of about 1600 BCE, showing a seaside community in oblique perspective, and an engraved map of the Babylonian city of Nippur from the Kassite period. The oldest surviving world maps are from Babylonia of the 9th century BCE; one shows Babylon on the Euphrates, surrounded by Assyria, Urartu and several cities, all encircled by a bitter river.

Cartography is the study and practice of making and using maps, combining science, aesthetics and technique. Its traditional objectives are to select the traits to be mapped, to represent terrain on flat media through map projections, to remove irrelevant characteristics through generalization, and to arrange the elements of the map to convey its message.

Maps are divided into general maps, made for a general audience, and thematic maps, which concern specific geographic themes, such as a map of corn production. A topographic map describes a place, with contour lines showing elevation, while a topological map disregards scale and detail to communicate route information; Beck's London Underground map is the usual example.

About 1,100 medieval European mappae mundi survive, of which some 900 illustrate manuscripts. In 1154 the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi produced his atlas Tabula Rogeriana, and his world map, mostly Ptolemaic in conception, remained the most accurate for the next three centuries. In 1492 Martin Behaim, advisor to King John II of Portugal, made the oldest extant globe, and Hartmann Schedel was among the first to use the printing press for maps.

The Selden map, made by a Chinese cartographer around 1620, though historians debate the date, shows trading routes, a compass rose and a scale bar. Enlightenment maps used copper plate intaglio rather than woodcut, and mapmakers often plagiarized: Herman Moll's Beaver Map of 1715 closely reproduces Nicolas de Fer's work of 1698. Some scholars argue that maps are inherently biased, and that cartography served imperial power in the conquest of Africa.
caspar-david-friedrich: Friedrich was the sixth of ten children, raised in the strict Lutheran creed of his father Adolf Gottlieb Friedrich, a candle-maker and soap boiler. Records of the family's finances are contradictory; some sources say the children were privately tutored, others that they lived in relative poverty. He knew death early: his mother Sophie died in 1781, a sister a year later, and another sister in 1791. In 1787 he witnessed his younger brother Johann Christoffer, aged thirteen, fall through the ice of a frozen lake and drown.

He studied in Copenhagen from 1794 to 1798, then settled permanently in Dresden. There he made etchings and designs for woodcuts, but he worked mainly in ink, watercolour and sepia, and did not work extensively in oils until his reputation was more established.

His landscapes, mostly of northern Germany, were inspired by trips from 1801 to the Baltic coast, Bohemia, the Krkonoše and the Harz Mountains. He made pencil studies of places such as the cliffs on Rügen and the Elbe, but rendered the atmospheric effects of mist, sun and moon from memory. His key innovation was to treat landscape not as a backdrop subordinated to human drama but as a self-contained emotive subject. He often used the Rückenfigur, a person seen from behind, to draw the viewer into sharing the contemplation of nature.

Resentment of the French occupation of Pomerania in 1813 led him to put motifs from German folklore in his work. In Old Heroes' Graves (1812) and Fir Forest with the French Dragoon and the Raven (c. 1813) he conveyed political symbols by means of the landscape alone, a first in the history of art. He suffered depressive episodes, and after 1826 vultures, owls, graveyards and ruins became permanent motifs, while his colours grew darker.
